definition: Blight means a disease that destroys growing plants.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word blight. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know blight should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: A blight reached the island's banana groves in June, and by harvest every plantation on the windward slope stood bare.
Mildew is far below blight — a gray film that dulls the leaf's surface and rarely kills the plant, where blight kills everything it spreads through.
Rot goes further than mildew — the tissue it touches dies — but blight claims the most: it races plant to plant and takes the whole field.

A canker is a localized sore — one wound on one branch or stem that the tree may simply grow around. A blight is never local: it is a disease that races plant to plant and takes whole plantings at once. A canker scars; a blight sweeps.

An infestation is an invasion of pests — beetles in the beams, mice in the walls — living things you can trap or spray. A blight is a disease inside the plants themselves, spreading through what it kills until the field is gone. Pests occupy; a blight infects.

Blight surfaced among English farmers and gardeners around 1600 with no traceable parent — no Latin root, no provable Old English ancestor. It names the destroyer without ever telling you where its own name came from, which somehow suits it.
Blight means a disease that destroys growing plants.
Wheat rust is a blight older than the alphabet; Roman farmers held a spring festival just to beg it away from their grain.
When a new race of the fungus appeared in Uganda in 1999, breeders watched it defeat one resistant variety after another, and seed banks on five continents began crossing wild grasses in a hurry.
A single infected stem can shed enough spores to sicken a whole district.
Blight is the exact word for rust, because a blight is a disease that destroys growing plants — and destroys is the operative claim.
Mildew films a leaf's surface and spoils its looks; rot takes the tissue it touches and stops there.
A blight travels, jumping plant to plant until whole harvests are gone.

In the summer of 1904, a forester at a New York zoo noticed the chestnut trees along the paths dying from the top down.
The cause was a fungal blight that had arrived quietly on imported nursery stock, and it moved with terrible speed.
Spores rode the wind, the rain, and the feet of birds; a single infected tree could doom a hillside within a few seasons.
By 1940 the blight had swept the entire eastern range, and a species that once numbered four billion trees was functionally gone.
Foresters could only watch: no spray reached the fungus under the bark, and no chestnut showed real resistance until breeders began crossing rare survivors decades later.
